In chapter 8, “The Queen’s Croquet-Ground,” the gardeners explain that the tree “ought to have been a
_red_ rose-tree, and we put a white one in by mistake”; they paint the roses before the Queen arrives because they fear what she’ll do if she finds out. Their situation involves an explicitly dangerous threat. It is not evidence about what your own reaction means.

Your saved note says you found the billing mistake was yours, fixed it over the weekend, said nothing on Monday, and keep telling yourself it was already handled. A study of nurses in hospital teams found that leader inclusiveness, safety climate, and psychological safety significantly affected willingness to report errors ([study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10599306/)). That research can offer a lens on speaking up, but it cannot establish why you stayed quiet; your note doesn’t state your reason either.

Perhaps the useful connection is the distinction between correcting an error and deciding whether to disclose it, without assuming the gardeners’ fear explains your reaction. When you imagine telling someone about it, what—if anything—does that seem to put at stake for you?

# A study of error reporting by nurses: the significant impact of nursing team dynamics

## Abstract

Background: Error reporting is crucial for organisational learning and improving patient safety in hospitals, yet errors are significantly underreported. Aims: The aim of this study was to understand how the nursing team dynamics of leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety affected the willingness of hospital nurses to report errors. Methods: The study was a cross-sectional design. Self-administered surveys were used to collect data from nurses and nurse managers. Data were analysed using linear mixed models. Bootstrap confidence intervals with bias correction were used for mediation analysis. Results: Leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety significantly affected willingness to report errors. Psychological safety mediated the relationship between safety climate and error reporting as well as the relationship between leader inclusiveness and error reporting.

## Introduction

Hospitals depend on employees to meaningfully contribute to quality improvement efforts by engaging in actions that foster organisational learning. Error reporting is a primary tool by which hospitals learn from mistakes and near misses that occur during the delivery of patient care. However, error reporting requires some degree of risk, whether real or perceived, on the part of the individuals who report error (Newman et al., 2017) . The existing literature demonstrates that errors and near misses in hospitals are significantly underreported (Levinson, 2012; Palmero et al., 2019; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Yung et al., 2016) . As a result, countless opportunities to improve patient care quality and safety are lost because some employees do not report errors and near misses when they occur. In this study, we examined how team dynamics on nursing units affected error reporting by nurses.

## Literature review

Error reporting is multifaceted, with myriad reasons that explain why the process of error reporting often breaks down. Much of past research in this area has examined the barriers to error reporting. This research has helped identify common structural barriers to error reporting, such as the complicated and time-consuming nature of error reporting systems, as well as knowledge deficits of what constitutes an error or a near miss (Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . Other studies have identified cultural and managerial barriers, and common fears about reporting errors that are often shared across different types of employees (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) .

While past studies have produced important findings, these findings have not fully explained how more complex factors within the organisation may affect error reporting by clinicians. Theory and research from organisational and team literature may help to better explain the more complex reasons as to why clinicians do or do not report errors, in a way that past research on error reporting has failed to do. # A study of error reporting by nurses: the significant impact of nursing team dynamics

## Abstract

Background: Error reporting is crucial for organisational learning and improving patient safety in hospitals, yet errors are significantly underreported. Aims: The aim of this study was to understand how the nursing team dynamics of leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety affected the willingness of hospital nurses to report errors. Methods: The study was a cross-sectional design. Self-administered surveys were used to collect data from nurses and nurse managers. Data were analysed using linear mixed models. Bootstrap confidence intervals with bias correction were used for mediation analysis. Results: Leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety significantly affected willingness to report errors. Psychological safety mediated the relationship between safety climate and error reporting as well as the relationship between leader inclusiveness and error reporting.

## Introduction

Hospitals depend on employees to meaningfully contribute to quality improvement efforts by engaging in actions that foster organisational learning. Error reporting is a primary tool by which hospitals learn from mistakes and near misses that occur during the delivery of patient care. However, error reporting requires some degree of risk, whether real or perceived, on the part of the individuals who report error (Newman et al., 2017) . The existing literature demonstrates that errors and near misses in hospitals are significantly underreported (Levinson, 2012; Palmero et al., 2019; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Yung et al., 2016) . As a result, countless opportunities to improve patient care quality and safety are lost because some employees do not report errors and near misses when they occur. In this study, we examined how team dynamics on nursing units affected error reporting by nurses.

## Literature review

Error reporting is multifaceted, with myriad reasons that explain why the process of error reporting often breaks down. # A study of error reporting by nurses: the significant impact of nursing team dynamics

## Abstract

Background: Error reporting is crucial for organisational learning and improving patient safety in hospitals, yet errors are significantly underreported. Aims: The aim of this study was to understand how the nursing team dynamics of leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety affected the willingness of hospital nurses to report errors. Methods: The study was a cross-sectional design. Self-administered surveys were used to collect data from nurses and nurse managers. Data were analysed using linear mixed models. Bootstrap confidence intervals with bias correction were used for mediation analysis. Results: Leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety significantly affected willingness to report errors. Psychological safety mediated the relationship between safety climate and error reporting as well as the relationship between leader inclusiveness and error reporting.

## Introduction

Hospitals depend on employees to meaningfully contribute to quality improvement efforts by engaging in actions that foster organisational learning. Error reporting is a primary tool by which hospitals learn from mistakes and near misses that occur during the delivery of patient care. However, error reporting requires some degree of risk, whether real or perceived, on the part of the individuals who report error (Newman et al., 2017) . The existing literature demonstrates that errors and near misses in hospitals are significantly underreported (Levinson, 2012; Palmero et al., 2019; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Yung et al., 2016) . As a result, countless opportunities to improve patient care quality and safety are lost because some employees do not report errors and near misses when they occur. In this study, we examined how team dynamics on nursing units affected error reporting by nurses.
